summary: This Standards Track document defines the JSContact Profiles IANA registry of named subsets of JSContact elements. It helps use JSContact in protocols or cases where supporting all semantics would be inappropriate.

eli5.summary: A big box of crayons, but you pick just a few colors for each drawing, and give each set a name.

questions: how to name a jscontact profile
subtitle: A registry of named, versioned subsets of JSContact so protocols can use just the parts they need.

tldr.problem: JSContact implementations are expected to support every element of the core specification, which can be inappropriate for protocols that only need some contact card information.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines a JSContact profile as a named, versioned list of property entries, and creates an IANA 'JSContact Profiles' registry to record them. Profiles can narrow property contexts, types, enum values and PatchObject keys, but never loosen restrictions.
tldr.outcome: Protocol designers can reuse JSContact instead of inventing a contact format, and library authors get one place to see which profile supports what. The registry starts empty.

today: RFC 10050 is a Proposed Standard published in September 2026. It has not been obsoleted or updated, and it relies on the JSContact format of RFC 9553.

sections.title: Why Profiles Are Needed
sections.content:
JSContact (RFC 9553) is a JSON contact card format meant as an alternative to vCard (RFC 6350). Implementations are expected to support all of its elements when exchanging cards over protocols such as CardDAV (RFC 6352) and JMAP for Contacts (RFC 9610).

Other protocols may need only some contact information. JSContact lets implementations ignore unknown elements, but that applies only to future extensions; they must still implement the whole core specification. This RFC adds JSContact profiles: named subsets of elements, listed in one IANA registry.
sections.eli5: Most programs do not need every single feature of a contact card. Profiles let them say which parts they actually care about.

sections.title: What a Profile Is
sections.content:
A profile is a named and versioned set of JSContact elements such as properties, types and values. The elements MUST be registered in the IANA 'JSContact' registry group. A profile MAY add restrictions but MUST NOT loosen them.

A JSContact object complies with a profile if all its properties are in the profile's set and the values meet the profile's restrictions. An object may comply with several profiles, so the RFC defines no way for data to say which profile it follows. Compliant data must still be valid under RFC 9553. How to handle valid but non-compliant data is protocol-specific; the RFC deliberately does not call it invalid.
sections.eli5: A profile is a rule book you can only make stricter. A drawing that follows the rule book is still a proper drawing, but a drawing that breaks it is not automatically wrong. Each game decides what to do about it.

sections.title: Profile Name and Version
sections.content:
A profile name contains only ASCII lowercase letters and digits, optionally separated by hyphens. It MUST start with a letter and be 1 to 255 characters long, matching the ABNF rule profile-name = lalpha *( ["-"] lalpha / DIGIT ).

Each profile is versioned independently. The version MUST be a positive integer, starts at 1, and MUST increase whenever the profile properties change.
sections.eli5: Each profile gets a short lowercase nickname and a version number, like 'soccer-rules version 2'. The number only goes up.

sections.title: Profile Properties
sections.content:
A profile holds a non-empty list of property entries. Each entry has these elements:

  • Property Name: a name from the 'JSContact Properties' registry. It may appear more than once, but entries must not conflict.
  • Property Context: the comma-separated object types where the property is supported, a subset of those registered.
  • Restricted Attributes: the only defined value is mandatory, which makes an optional property required.
  • Restricted Property Type: pins the type to its original definition, or restricts an A|B union to a subset, such as PartialDate|Timestamp down to PartialDate.
  • Restricted Enum Values: limits enumerated values to a listed subset.
  • Restricted PatchObject: yes means each JSON Pointer key must be a single reference token.

All profiles support @type and version, so profiles must not include entries for them.
sections.eli5: Each line in the list says one thing: 'this field is allowed here, it must be filled in, and it can only be one of these choices'.

sections.title: Working Out the Supported Properties
sections.content:
The supported set is computed in steps. First, start with every Card property that has an entry with Card in its context; if there is none, start with all IANA-registered Card properties. Second, for each property whose value is an object type (or a list, map or union of object types), add the properties that have entries for those types, or all registered properties of those types when no entry exists. Third, repeat until every object type reached has been considered.

A Card complies if all its properties are supported and their values meet the entries' restrictions. A PatchObject MUST NOT patch unsupported properties.
sections.eli5: Start with the main list, then look at every sub-list it points to, and keep going until there is nothing new to look at. If a sub-list has no special rule, you get all of it.

sections.title: The Example Profile
sections.content:
Appendix A builds an illustrative profile that is not registered with IANA. It allows cards only for individuals and organizations, address lines only through the mandatory full property, full names and name components, all email address properties, birthday anniversaries restricted to PartialDate, and localizations whose PatchObject may only replace Card properties.

The RFC shows a compliant Card, a fictive registry entry named jscontact-simple-example at version 1, and a step-by-step walk through the supported-property algorithm for this profile.
sections.eli5: The example is a pretend rule book for a simple address book, with a worked sample showing a card that follows it.

sections.title: The JSContact Profiles Registry
sections.content:
IANA created the 'JSContact Profiles' registry inside the 'JSContact' registry group. Adding a new profile name or version needs 'Specification Required'. Updating the references of an existing entry needs 'Expert Review'. The change controller is the IETF. Every entry has a Name, a Version and a Reference, and Name and Version cannot change after creation.

Designated experts check that the name is unique, the entries are syntactically valid, only known property names are used, type restrictions do not alter a type incorrectly, and the version increases. They do not decide the profile's contents. The registry has no initial contents. The Security Considerations say the document adds nothing new and that those of RFC 9553 apply.
sections.eli5: A librarian checks that each new rule book has a fresh name, is written correctly and has a higher version than before. The librarian does not decide what the rules say.

data.title: profile-name ABNF
data.code:
profile-name = lalpha *( ["-"] lalpha / DIGIT )
               ; at most 255 characters in size

lalpha       = %x61-7A ; a-z
